utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, learned counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood for the Prosecution assisted by Alma Imamovic-Ivanov our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. Yes, and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, good afternoon to my colleagues from the Prosecution. I'm Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Delic with our case manager Lana Deljkic. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe there is some housekeeping that somebody wants to raise. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to draw your attention to two brief issues. The first issue relates again to the material falling under Rule 68; and the second issue has to do with the material from the Italian collection. One of the issues that the Trial Chamber considered and is still considering and that the Defence has raised is the issue of other Arab units involved in the events which are in the charges of this indictment and is specifically the group Abu Zubeir. The Defence understands the significance of this group, and in the course of the preparation for this case, it has insisted on receiving all the material that the Prosecutor had at his disposal, especially those relating to Rule 68 and also those relating to Rule 66 (B). On the 27th of June, 2007, as part of a batch of documents that was forwarded to us under number 49, the Prosecutor, in keeping with Rule 68, specifically for the folder of General Delic forwarded the results after the search that was done by ES for the Abu Zubeir group. After this the Prosecutor forwarded various materials in relation to or under Rule 68 in batches. On the 18th of March, after the completion of the testimony of witness DV 4 and you will recall, Your Honour that is correct this witness, among other things, testified specifically about the role of the Abu Zubeir unit. He testified that morning and on the same day in the afternoon we received a large batch of documents that related to Abu Zubeir. As one of the documents within that batch, Your Honour, was document 04174457 consisting of three pages which had in no way before the moment that we received it then forwarded to the Defence it was not in the EDS system it was not in the specific folder nor was it in any other way forwarded to us while we were preparing this witness. Why am I mentioning this document, Your Honour. I am mentioning it because DV 4 and also witness Zilkic specifically testified about something that mention is made of in this document. DV 4, if you recall, Your Honour, was the leader of one of the units. In this document specifically the mention is made that the Abu Zubeir group had the support of this unit. This is a fact that I wasn't aware of, obviously the Prosecutor was and instead of forwarding the document to me a few days before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say Abu Zubeir had the support of this unit -- or can you repeat that part. I'm not quite sure who had the support of which unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps it didn't enter the transcript. Abu Zubeir, according to this document, had the support of the unit at the head of which was the witness who had testified here on Friday. Now, this fact was something that the Defence had no knowledge of. The Prosecutor obviously did know about this, because we received this document in the afternoon after his testimony. What is also of great concern to the Defence and a very important issue that Defence is dealing wit, and that the Defence explored with several witnesses is that in this document specific mention is made of the fact that the Abu Zubeir unit in the combat operations that it participated in had the support of the Asim Camgic unit. I believe, Your Honour, that you will recall that this unit, unit Asim Camgic was subordinate to witness Asim Zilkic. It is certain, Your Honour, that had I this document, I would had -- at that time I would have asked some additional questions to the witness Zilkic and I believe the court would have probably have done the same thing. Your Honour, I would like to draw your attention and I appeal to you at this point because I have been informed that the Prosecutor has submitted a reply to our motion under Rule 68. I would appreciate the Trial Chamber making their ruling on this motion, because we will find ourselves in a position where we have found ourselves in, that our witnesses have already gone, been here and gone, and we have been unable to show them, to confront them with the documents under Rule 68 so that they can make a comment on them. Your Honour, I have to repeat now, we are considering the situation very seriously, because this is something that may affect the entire proceedings. The trial will not be fair if we are unable to have the documents that are exculpatory and to use them. This will not only be our problem alone but also a problem that this Trial Chamber will have to deal with. That is one issue relating to Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go any further. Can we deal this and finish with it first and before I ask Mr. Mundis to stand up, can I just spell this name for the Stenographer because I see every time it is mentioned it is not being typed in here. It's Abu Zubeir, A-b-u, next word, Z-u-b-e-i-r, Abu Zubeir. Okay. Mr. Mundis, any response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No, we don't have any specific response. We filed a response to the Defence motion. We've also submitted a letter to them. I believe that was copied to the Chamber's legal officer. At this point in time we have nothing further to add on this specific document or on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I for one have not seen the letter that you have copied to the Chamber. But over and above the motion, the motion about Rule 68 disclosures, Madam Vidovic is raising this issue, I'm not quite sure -- well, I guess the gist of what she is saying is that she's getting documents after her witnesses have testified, and are you able to say whether or not she will get these documents in time henceforth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will indicate as I've said before that we are in the process of undertaking a top-to-bottom review including running some additional and new searchs. I'm unable at this point on my feet here to answer the question as to which specific search resulted in the particular document that Madam Vidovic has mentioned. I also indicated at the pre-Defence conference that we would run ISU searchs on Defence witness names in the order that those were to be scheduled and it is possible that the particular document that Madam Vidovic has mentioned was in response to one of those ISU searches and I have indicated, the more advance notice we have of the actual calendar, the quicker we'll be able to get those results. I can assure everyone in this courtroom that under no circumstances is the Office of the Prosecutor sitting on documents and waiting in terms of timing of disclosing them under Rule 68 for any kind of tactical or strategic advantage. Obviously Rule 68 is a serious issue. I have stated that before here in this courtroom. It is obviously an ongoing obligation that will continue until this institution closes and probably even beyond that date. So the fact that Rule 68 material is being disclosed now is par for the course. We will continue disclosing Rule 68 material as that material is identified and/or as that material comes into the possession of the Prosecutor. With respect, Your Honour, to the letter that I referred to, that is attached to our filing of the 20th of March as Annex A to that filing and I understand because of the holiday weekend I'm not sure if that was distributed until today but I did sign off that on I believe it was Thursday, the 20th and it was filed after hours electronically so that to the extent that has not yet been distributed, it should be in the process of being distributed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, your request is that the Trial Chamber rules on the Rule 68 motion. You're not asking for any ruling now on what you have just said, as I understand you. Okay. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We will do our best to get to that as soon as we possibly can. We always try to give our rulings or decisions as quickly as possible after all filings have been filed. And I can assure you that we will do the same. Okay. You may proceed then to the next point, Italian material, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just one sentence as concerns this issue, I would also like this to be on the record, this problem, because I have to reply at least in one sentence to what Mr. Mundis said. In this case it was not about the name of the witness. If -- so that an ISU search of the name would produce the document. No, it was about the Abu Zubeir group and this has been the subject of this trial throughout this time and I would just like to point to this Chamber that this may have a significant effect on the proceedings, and everything that the Prosecutor failed to forward to the Defence and the Defence was unable to use, I would apply for each document, such document to be used and that the Trial Chamber make a ruling in favour of the accused on those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic -- yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, I do have just one additional point or two additional points. Prior to this trial commencing, I met with Madam Vidovic and we agreed upon pre-trial Rule 68 terms which included Abu Zubeir spelled in two variations of that name, one being Z-u-b-e-i-r, and the second spelling being Abu Zubair, Z-u-b-a-i-r. It is my understanding that the document which was just turned over a week ago had the spelling Z-u-b-e-j-r. Again, we have the same problems in terms much conducting electronic searchs that many of us in dealing with this type of case have had in terms of the way the names are spelled and/or transliterated from Arabic into the Bosnian language and the way those names are spelled in documents, so that is a problem that neither the Defence nor the Prosecution fully appreciated because although we gave two various of spelling on the name Abu Zubeir, we did not anticipate or expect that there would be an alternative spelling, b-e-j-r, and that's the document that was turned up in this most recent search. Turning to the more general issue the Defence has raised, we have indicated both in our response to their motion and I indicated orally I believe it was last week that in the event the Defence seeks to tender some or all of these documents from the bar table, the Prosecution was not likely to object to that, so if the Defence has a list of documents that they would propose tendering that was a direct result of delayed Rule 68 disclosure, I would be happy to sit down and discusses that with the Defence or if she were to file a motion or send me a letter we will respond accordingly, but again I'm not going to stand here and indicate that we would oppose the Defence tendering such documents from the bar table assuming that they were from this collection of material that was recently disclosed in which the Defence believes constitutes Rule 68 material. So I want to make that very clear as I have in the past so that there is absolutely no confusion about that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I think we have heard all that we can hear about this issue. Can we move on to the Italian material, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just recall the fact that the Trial Chamber, upon our motion, issued an order to the government of Italy on the 23rd of January, 2008, that's two months ago. We reiterated this issue, if you recall, at the 65 (G) conference exactly a month and Your Honours had undertaken then to take further steps to have the government of Italy comply with the order. I must draw your attention to the fact that to date, after numerous interventions made before the government of Italy to get these documents, although the Prosecutor did not have any such problem, they said they wrote a letter, investigators went to Italy and just received the materials they wanted. That being so I cannot understand that the government of a country who is a member of the United Nations and a signatory of the UN charter of human rights completely the requests of this Defence team and does not even react to the orders of the Trial Chamber. I must kindly ask Your Honour to do what you indicated you would do earlier, namely, take further steps to make the government of Italy produce these documents we believe are exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Vidovic, thank you so much, we did hear what you said and we promise you the Chamber will look in the matter as soon as possible. Is that all that you have to say? Anything from your side? Can we call the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Defence calls Major-General Vahid Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May you please make the declaration the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Thank you so much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, General Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start with the questioning, I would like to ask you to speak slowly so that the record reflect exactly every word. Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, would you tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: My name is Vahid Karavelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Any nicknames?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Vaha.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: V-a-h-a, Vaha.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: 7th of April, 1956, in Brezovik, Visoko municipality, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your occupation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Former officer, currently retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which schooling have you completed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The Military Academy, for ground forces in Belgrade; and then the school of material management in the USA; and post-graduate studies in Sarajevo, the University of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell the Trial Chamber, if you had testified before this Tribunal before, and if so, in what cases?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did testify before. In the case of Stanislav Galic; in the Dragomir Milosevic case; in the Sefer Halilovic case; and in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, kindly tell us did you appear as a Prosecution witness or a Defence witness in the cases in which you testified.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the Galic and Dragomir Milosevic case I appeared as a Prosecution witness. In the Hadzihasanovic case, I was subpoenaed as a witness of the Court and in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case I appeared as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You seem to have said that in the Hadzihasanovic case you appeared as a witness of the Court and in a different capacity in the same case and that you were subpoenaed. In which case were you subpoenaed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the Sefer Halilovic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you where were you serving in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army serving in Slovenia, more precisely, the city of Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did the beginning of the war find you and did you at any moment join the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was there, and I was a member. In fact, I joined the Territorial Defence, later the BiH army on the 6th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What position did you occupy in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was one of the first to be appointed commander in that new Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, commander of the District Staff of Territorial Defence of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What rank did you have when you left the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, were you a member of any political organisation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties in the Territorial Defence? In fact you told us that. What were your duties in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if any?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: After I was exchanged, I became one of the operative officers in the Main Staff of the BH army, and I did that until the 1st of September, 1992. From that time until July 1993, I was assistant commander of the 1st corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. When were you exchanged? When were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was exchanged on the 13th of May, 1992, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Exchanged from what to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used to be commander of the District Staff of the Territorial Defence of Tuzla in April, when the war began. That's when I was captured by the enemy. That is the former Yugoslav People's Army. They took me to Belgrade. Put me in the prison of Sremska Mitrovica and then I got lucky. First I was sentenced to death but then I was returned to Sarajevo by helicopter in order to be exchanged against a large number of their officers who had been captured by the defenders of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I was intending to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that for a while you were assistant commander of the 1st Corps of the BiH. After that did you discharge any other duties?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: After that position, beginning with July 1993 until August 1995, I was commander of the 1st Corps of the BH army. And after that I took up the position of chief of operations. Later it became the administration for planning and operations in the army of the BH Federation, and I remained in that post until I was retired in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the beginning of your testimony you mentioned that in 1990 you were serving in Slovenia. Could you explain why you were transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I was transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina because all the units of the Yugoslav People's Army were withdrawing from the territory of Slovenia and even Croatia. They were withdrawing to Bosnia and Herzegovina, to areas with a majority Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember to which area of Bosnia and Herzegovina you arrived then?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: With my unit and my military assets, I came to Zenica, in the central part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the 20th of August, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained that the Yugoslav People's Army withdraw from Slovenia and Croatia. Do you remember what happened to the weaponry of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: As the units were withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia, all the military equipment and assets of the JNA were being pulled out as well and taken to Bosnia and Herzegovina. With my unit, I got stationed in Zenica, and a large amount of assets, 250 military vehicles, 13 trains and many other transports of weaponry were taken to Kalnik, close to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened to those weapons?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: For the most part, those weapons were distributed to the units formed by Serbian politicians, comprising of Serbs in Serb villages. I also believe that any surplus of weaponry was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the situation in terms of weapons as regards the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: At that time since I could foretell what will follow and since I was in Bosnia and Herzegovina I was quite amazed at the situation that the non-Serb population of Bosnia and Herzegovina found itself in. They had nothing whatsoever apart from hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the Security Council of the UN, concerning the process of arming in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Of course the Security Council of the UN, as far as I can recall, on the 25th of September, 1991, pronounced a resolution number 713, ordering any further transport of military equipment and weapons in the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, prohibiting any further transport.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show video number 36 to the witness at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General Karavelic, I'd like you to -- to ask you the following. Can you provide any comment concerning the ratio mentioned in the footage and the amount of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I have seen this footage countless times, even during the war, all of the footage was made by the Bosnia-Herzegovina Television. I believe it is completely authentic, and it fully reflects the situation as it existed at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I believe it to have been even far more severe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning this footage, I wanted to ask you the following. You heard that the arms embargo was mentioned and you heard that there was a UN resolution in place concerning the embargo itself. Who was the embargo -- who did the embargo hit the most?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The embargo only hit the forces loyal to the government of the internationally recognised Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, in turn, means that most of its population were Bosnians, or rather, Bosniaks as well as Croats and Serbs who were loyal to the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Serb forces and the Croat forces were not damaged by the embargo, since they had sufficient weaponry at their disposal. They also enjoyed the support from Belgrade and Zagreb respectively.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to stay with the embargo a bit longer. In your view, did it have -- did the embargo have any impact on the rest of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina until its very end?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That embargo had a lot of influence upon the war, because at the very outset of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, the aggressor had enormous quantities of weaponry and equipment whereas those defending the country were basically unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to tender this footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, just before we tender, can we just play it once -- one more time. Not all of it. Let's just play it and I will ask you to stop where I have a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Stop. Earlier we saw TV SA. Now it says HTV. You say which television channel is this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatian Television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought earlier in answer to a question by Madam Vidovic you said it was Bosnia-Herzegovina Television. Was that a mistake, or did I mishear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that most of the footage was made by Bosnia-Herzegovina Television. However, I still believe this footage to have been shown on Bosnia-Herzegovina television, probably Croatia television carried it as well. Therefore, I don't know where this particular copy was taken from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But who photographed this? Who took this footage life on the ground, your knowledge, if you do know. Was it the Bosnian television and then it was played by the Croatian television or was it taken by the Croatian television and then copied by the Bosnian television, which is which?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where is it from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to tell you precisely. I have some understanding of the process. Either of the TV stations could have done that. I don't know where this particular footage was broadcast. That is the issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look at this still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try and clarify one detail, Your Honour. Do you recognise the still? Is this a town that you know?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This still shows a mosque being hit. I believe it was the Sokolje mosque in a neighbourhood of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender the footage now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video becomes the exhibit number 1322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that at the beginning of the war you commanded the TO District Staff for Tuzla. Briefly, briefly, tell us how TO units were formed; that is, the TO of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I can put it in a single sentence. They were formed from grass root level. If you need any further clarification, I can go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Clarify briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: So they were formed from bottom up. All armies of the world as a rule are formed from top down. Ours was formed from the bottom, because the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina that had existed saw over 70 per cent of its organisational structure damaged or disrupted. As such, it could no longer carry the responsibilities and tasks. Quite the contrary, we had to initiate the formation of units in neighbourhoods, streets, villages, parts of towns, where we had brave lads who could assemble people. And they, in turn, became leaders and commanders, that's how we were constructing our army. At some point, we only recognised a unit that had already been formed, appointing the commander who had organised the unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This way of forming units, what impact did it have on the establishing of the system of command and control?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Because the army was formed that way, later on we had severe malfunctions of its command and control system as well as overall discipline. When one forms an army in that way, we see brave people commanding units but also people who are prone to be less disciplined and to go against the law. This had severe consequences for the overall army discipline throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you know, and remember, or let me put it this way, do you remember when an order for the formation of the corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was issued?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the first such order of the Supreme Command was on the 18th of August, 1992. In early September, we started working on the formation of the corps. That same year, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain. Was this order implemented immediately or did a process of sorts followed?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That order was merely a piece of paper. In order to be able to implement it in full, in peacetime conditions, for example to establish a corps, one needs at least a year or more. Given the wartime conditions that Bosnia-Herzegovina was in as well as its army, we needed far more time than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, did the members of the BH army in the first years of the war have ranks?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the first two wars [as interpreted] of the war, our officers, the officers of the BH army, did not have any ranks. If I can add, the main reason for that was because ranks could not be bestowed because of inadequate professional training of the men who were heading the units. Because the total number, speaking in percentages, was about 2 to 3 per cent of the men who had completed some military school.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which first two wars did you refer to here, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which wars are those? Can you call them by name or against whom were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really apologise, I do not get your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may assist, it is an interpretation error. If I understand this correctly, this means that somebody was aware that the interpretation was incorrect. The witness did not mention two wars but the first two years of the war. And if necessary, we can repeat this. This is what is causing the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you do see line 17 at page 19. Is that what you are correcting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I can confirm that I heard the translation "years" and not "wars." It may have come out because of the stenography but that's a technical -- no, I'm not blaming you, that's the way your machine works sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks for the correction. I was looking at the transcript. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned a percentage. You said point -- you said 2.5 to 3 per cent of the people were -- of the officers had military training in the BH army. Tell us, please, can we put this in some time-frame, was this throughout the war or were you referring to the first two years of the war? Can we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This situation, in the BH army, remained throughout the war the same. But in 1994 and 1995, so in the last two years of the war, we tried to educate a part of our officer corps; we tried to train them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In the beginning of your testimony you mentioned that the Yugoslav People's Army had taken away the military assets, the weaponry and the equipment, and distributed it to the Serbian population. Do you remember who provided logistic support during the war to the BH army, or how was the logistic support provided to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, the overall supplies and logistics were provided by the local authorities on the ground. Only towards the end of the war a partial equipment and supplies were provided from the top, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify this. When you say "local authorities on the ground," could you tell us, please, what kind of authorities are you talking about? Are these military or political authorities? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: When I said that, I mean -- I meant primarily the civilian authorities, the local communes, the municipalities, people, civilians, powerful people and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I will have to ask you again, because the transcript does not reflect your reply. Could you please -- the question was, were these military or political authorities and you did provide an answer, but it is not clear from the transcript. Could you tell us briefly were these military or civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: These were civilian authorities at the local commune level and then municipalities, individual citizens, wealthy citizens and so on. They provided support.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will come back to this question later. Now I would like to ask you about something else. You mentioned that you were the assistant commander, corps commander, from September 1st, 1992. Do you remember what was the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 1st Corps of the BH army, I can tell you which municipalities they cover. It was the Sarajevo city itself, the Stari Grad municipality, Centar municipality, Novo Sarajevo municipality, Novi Grad municipality, a part of Ilidza municipality, Trnovo municipality, a part of Hadzici municipality, Fojnica municipality, Visoko municipality, Breza municipality, Vares municipality, Olovo municipality, a part of Ilijas municipality and later on it also included the Zepa and Gorazde municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said Zepa and Gorazde. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the 1st Corps command during the war?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The 1st Corps command during the war briefly was on the territory of Novo Sarajevo municipality, and then from the end of 1992 up until the end of the war it was in the Centar municipality, very close to the Supreme Command and the General Staff, more precisely in Danijela Ozme street at number 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What you're trying to tell us is that the command of the Main Staff was also in Sarajevo. Was my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where the commander of the Main Staff was, in what building was his office?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff commander was on the premises of the Vranica building company.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember where, between June 1993 up until the end of the war was the administration of military security of the Main Staff of the BH army, or, rather, the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It was on the promises of the court-house in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the courts," or "court-house," do you recall which court this was?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I don't know whom this building belonged to, whether this was the cantonal court or the municipal court, one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So this was not the building of the state court?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether in the Main Staff of the BH army in June 1993, there were some changes, and, if so, what were they? Did you, as a member of command of the 1st Corps, did you know of this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In June 1993, the Supreme Command adopted a decision to restructure the Main Staff to change its structure. A new function was introduced at that time, the role of the commander of the Main Staff, which was later to be the General Staff of the BH army, of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when this happened?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I think this was on 8 June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly how did you find out about this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I found out when my commander, the commander of the 1st Corps, Mustafa Hajrulohovic, also known as Talijan, called me and told me to join him to a meeting. The meeting had, as its role -- the meeting was to inaugurate on this position the general of the Main Staff Sefer Halilovic as the Chief of Staff in that command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when this meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I think the meeting was in the evening about 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at one point you were a member of the Patriotic League. Do you remember what was the reaction of the Patriotic League members when they heard of the change of the commander, if any? Change in the command and the commander.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Patriotic League and this meeting, if that's what we're talking about, the directive from the Supreme Command was issued by the then member of parliament, Mr. Konjicija, he read this directive and then all of us who were present there started a discussion amongst us about this. I have to say that most people were reasonable and accepted General Delic as the new commander, as the first man in the army. However, a number of people protested and did not immediately warm to this fact. I can mention, for instance Rifat Belijac as one such man, Zicro Suljevic, Kemo Karisik. All these men later became generals and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please kindly repeat these names because it is important for them to be written down in the transcript. Could you please repeat them?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: General Zicro Silvoc, General Rifat Belijac, and General Meho Karisik, aka Kemo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please spell it and those names that you mentioned, could you please just spell them, because it's really important for this to enter?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Zicro Suljevic, Z-i-c-r-o S-u-l-j-e-v-i-c, Rifat Bilajac, R-i-f-a-t B-i-l-a-j-a-c, and Meho Karisik, M-e-h-o K-a-r-i-s-i-k, aka Kemo, K-e-m-o.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last sentence, because it's time for our break, could you please tell us what was the reaction of the man, the first man in the staff up until then. Who was the first man in the staff up until then?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The reaction was very negative, a bit aggressive. Personally, when it was my turn to comment on this, I invited this man to submit to the decision -- to defer to the decision of the Supreme Command and the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and he said to me then, Well, you too, Brutus?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell me who said that to you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So Halilovic was also against the appointment of General Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he was the one who most strenuously and vociferously objected and he was the ring leader of the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to make sure that his name was properly registered as someone who was opposed to the appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is past time. Shall we take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, there's one little point before you proceed which I wanted to clarify. Sir, you said that the meeting was held on the evening of the -- on the 8th of June, 1993. And you said in that meeting what was Halilovic inaugurated as, as the Chief of Staff in the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the new post created in the establishment, yes. Although he had discharged those functions even until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And Delic was appointed as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is precisely because the whole structure was changed. Until then, Sefer Halilovic was the first man of the army. When the main command was changed in structure a new post was introduced, following orders of the Supreme Command and that was the duty of the commander of the Main Staff, and General Delic occupied it. Sefer Halilovic opposed this move because he was no longer the first man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask. You have spoken of the evening of the 8th of June. Could you be more precise, Witness, giving us more or less the time when this meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it was between the 1900 hours and 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Earlier you had said it was at 8.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say that. I said I thought it was at 8.00 p.m. whether it started at 7.00 or 8.00 or 8.30, but it is within that time span.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It didn't start earlier then, sir, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would now like to discuss with you the month of June 1993. Could you briefly, but very briefly indeed, describe the military situation around Sarajevo in June 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In June 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Witness. Give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we should like to give the witness a map and ask him to mark several locations, because we find that we waste a lot of time with electronic maps. Therefore, we want the map on the ELMO so that we are able to follow what the witness is saying. It's D1002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Karavelic, there is some unclarity about the meetings that took place on the 8th of June and at which time they took place and what happened during these meetings, and it has some importance to the case. So, therefore, in order to clarify, I would like you to answer to the following questions. First of all, do you know when General Delic was officially appointed by, I suppose, the president of the Presidency, to the position as chief of the Main Staff on -- commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Delic was appointed by the Supreme Commander perhaps a day or two earlier, but the official inauguration of General Delic as number one in the BH army was on that day, the 8th of June, 1993, at that meeting. When the decision of the Supreme Commander was brought by Mr. Konjicija, Member of Parliament, who read out the decision appointing General Delic commander of the Main Staff of the BH army, while Sefer Halilovic was to remain in the post that he occupied until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, I understand that Mr. Konjicija, Member of Parliament, read out a decision appointing General Delic as commander of the Main Staff. Can you tell me whether this was the public announcement of this appointment and if this was the public announcement of the assignment, whether then at some earlier point General Delic had been officially appointed. Do you understand my question? If you do not understand, then please tell me and then I will try and rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I understood. I don't know exactly the date on that order of the Supreme Command appointing General Delic commander of the Main Staff. It's probably dated the same day, but I'm not sure, or maybe a day earlier. I don't know when the Supreme Commander had a meeting, but it's very important that he took up his duties only at the moment when the decision was publicly announced and broadcast by the media, not before. And when it was announced to his subordinates, generals and officers, and that was that evening, the 8th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was just saying what happened to me at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who else was present; do you recall? Or let me put my question slightly differently. Was it a meeting attended by many people or was it a closed circle of officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An inner circle of officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so do you recall who else was present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to me there was commander of the 1st Corps Mustafa Hajrulohovic, known as Talijan; there was Mr. Konjicija, General Delic, Sefer Halilovic, there was Rifat Bilajac, Meho Karisik, Fikret Muslimovic, Rifat Bilajac, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. So let me just make sure that I understand you correctly. Your position is that General Delic did not assume control over the army, according to his newly established -- his newly appointed function until the evening of the 8th of June, around, say, 8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And as of that moment, Halilovic, General Halilovic was then just told to stay in his position or was he offered another position as a Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was told that he was to remain in that position but to accept General Delic as his commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And my final question is: Do you recall where exactly the meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the room. It was in the room that used to be occupied by the man number 1 of the army, Sefer Halilovic, in the court-house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So is this General Halilovic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it was an office, whether it was his office or it was a larger room. I couldn't tell with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In which building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court-house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, you already said that, I'm sorry, I missed that. Thank you very much, sir. You may proceed, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And thank you, General. I wanted to ask you about the military situation in Sarajevo in June 1993, the time you were describing just now. From that moment that you've just described until the end of June, or rather, the end of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: June 1993, at that time the city was under uninterrupted blockade for 18 months already. Day in day out, every day the aggressor forces attacked the city, aiming to cut off various neighbourhoods, one from another, and thus occupy it. The city was under constant shelling, targeting civilian targets, and thousands of sniper infantry weapons and other projectiles were fired everyday. In the area where I was, in my corps, the command and control were completely disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, madam. Can you just read the question that you put to the question and tell us whether it is correctly transcribed, in particular with respect to dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It's not quite correct. I asked about the military situation around Sarajevo in June 1993 and until the end of July 1993. So it was not correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand that I asked you about June and July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at this time we would like to show the video-clip number 38 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the witness. Your Honours, I would like the map to remain there because the witness will be using it later.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, about this video, I want to you ask if you recognise the scenes you saw in this clip.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I do. I recognise all of them, and I eye-witnessed most of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about June and July 1993. Is this the time of such events, like those we see on the video?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Precisely that's the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we give this exhibit a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What -- what city is this that is being attacked?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witnesses, can you tell us what city is this?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: All the footage we have seen are of attacks on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The tape is admitted into evidence. May it please be given a number. What did you say that number of the video was? V what?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The video-clip was 38.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video becomes exhibit number 1323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you now mark Sarajevo on the map.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to draw on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just put a little circle around the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to encircle the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not defence lines. The city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether we are being shown the -- let me see, okay. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, General, you told us a moment ago that the city was under siege, constant siege. Could you tell us how it was possible to exit from the city of Sarajevo in June and July 1993, if at all?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992 and 1993, it was very difficult, almost impossible, to enter or get out of Sarajevo, because the city was under complete and full military siege by the aggressor forces. The only way where individual crossings in and out were possible was to run across in inclement weather across the airport, that is the run way of the airport, because the airport was under the control of the UNPROFOR. However, if the individuals were noticed by the UNPROFOR, they would be apprehended and taken back. Along the airport, along the length of the airport aggressor forces had their line shooting at the airport. It was very difficult for anyone to cross without being injured or wounded or even killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I asked you specifically about June and July 1993, and I want to ask the following. What you have just described, does it also apply to June and July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Of course it applies to both June and July. But in June and especially July, even when an individual manages to get across the run way, later on, if they attempt to reach the free territory in the central part of Bosnia, they would have to cross Mount Igman and that was another point of high risk, not less so than the airport run way. Mount Igman was also under attack by the aggressor whose aim was to create a perfect encirclement of the city. Mount Igman was also under strong fire by the enemy 24 hours a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that a tunnel was dug somewhere there and if you remember it, give us the date?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: We called it the Sarajevo War Tunnel. We dug it exactly on the 31st of July; that is, the night of 31st July, under the airport run way.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just described how risky it was to attempt to get out of Sarajevo and you explained what municipalities were within the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps. Now could you please tell us what communications were possible with units outside of Sarajevo. Try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Communications with units outside of Sarajevo, any kind of communication, was scarce. There was no continuity, there were frequent and long breakdowns and the means of communications were very poor. So communications were sporadic and unsafe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was this tunnel dug and completed on one day, on the 31st of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The building of the tunnel began back in end of February that same year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you said it was dug exactly on the 31st of July, do you mean that was the end -- the completion date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used the word that actually means that the two sides of the tunnel dug by two different sets of our soldiers met at that point in the night of the 31st of July. And that's considered to be the completion of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you the following. You said you were appointed commander of the 1st Corps in July 1993. Was there any cooperation between you as the corps commander and the command of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Between me as commander of the 1st Corps in the city of Sarajevo where I was located, where I was based, there was soldierly and professional cooperation with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, actually, my drift was a bit different. I wanted to ask you if you met with members of the command of the Main Staff, including the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you discuss, what were the subjects of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Current military activities and how to defend Sarajevo as a strategic point, both for the aggressor and the defenders.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now based on these discussions, were you able to evaluate the level of information available to the General Staff about free territories. That is, those outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that based on my own experience because half of my corps was encircled in the city of Sarajevo and the other half was outside of Sarajevo. I was only superficially informed about that other half of my corps, and therefore I can confirm that the commander of the General Staff had very sparse information about the status of other corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss it with him occasionally?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what he would tell you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I was thinking about how to improve communications, how to get by -- by more up-to-date devices, how to left the siege around Sarajevo and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go to the 10th of June and the period until the 30th of June, 1993. I wish that a document be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will stay with the map throughout the testimony. Now I would like to have D931 shown, please. For the transcript it is a document from the 1st Corps command dated the 13th of June, 1993. The title is: Amendment to combat report forwarded to the staff of the Supreme Command. Witness, this is a short document. I can quote it to you, since it is difficult to read: "In the area of responsibility of IBOG Gorazde, according to the last extraordinary report the situation is alarming. The last defence lines on the right bank were broken through; Chetniks are entering the town; there are hundreds of killed and wounded. They have nothing else left to resist the Chetniks with. Everything is being demolished, burned down and people being killed. There is no control or resistance on the right bank of the Drina. They are requesting us to do everything we can in order to try and protect the remaining population." I want to ask you this. You mentioned Gorazde as one of the places being in the AOR of your corps. What would be your comment as to the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: My comment would be this. It reflects for the most part the situation, although there is no such a document which could truly paint the picture of the situation in Gorazde at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is mentioned here is a Serb offensive. What was the aim of that offensive, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I do very well. I was one of the people engaged in the defence and fighting the offensive. In early June, the offensive began by the aggressor aimed at the eastern Bosnian enclaves, that is, Gorazde. It was ongoing combat. Lines were being broken through and the aggressor was occupying more and more of our territory. The role, or the aim, was to carry on with the offensive and to cut off the corridor leading to Gorazde and later on to occupy Bijelasnica, Trnovo, Treskavica, and Igman so as to encircle Sarajevo with a second ring. They also continued their attacks from Vogosca to Zuc to force the military and political leaders to a dead-end position.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time of this, were you in contact with the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the commander and the Main Staff try to deal with these problems?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In such poor communications conditions, they tried to establish communication with the units involved and to try and replenish the forces defending Sarajevo. There were also trying to improve logistics and sending its officers to assist in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please assign an exhibit number to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Document D 931 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: General, I would kindly ask you to locate Gorazde on the map before you. I believe we can see it on the ELMO. Please find Gorazde and mark it.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Gorazde is inside the circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please see that on the screen. Thank you. I would like to ask you the following. What was the result of the offensive you've just described?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The result of the offensive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam Vidovic. I heard the witness say Gorazde is inside the circle. Is he able to show us where it is inside the circle. And just secondly draw the smaller circle. Right, fine, okay. Now we can see it. Sorry. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you to share with us what the result of the offensive was, the offensive undertaken by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The result of that offensive on the part of the aggressor was that between Trnovo and Gorazde, they completely took over the corridor area. That corridor was used by the population of Gorazde to supply themselves with things they needed up until that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please put a circle around Trnovo. You mentioned that. You mentioned the corridor. Please mark Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This is the town of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the corridor on the map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: No. Not on this one. But I can draw a line to indicate where it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said ... if I understood you well, you said that the corridor was cut off in the offensive.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Along the whole stretch, because Trnovo was occupied as well as the Rogoj mountain pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, General. Let us have a look at D 936 next and then I will ask you to mark some things on the map. General, before we see the document, I would like to ask you to mark Rogoj.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This is the Rogoj mountain pass. It is a very important feature. The trig point is 1163.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us have a look at D 936 next please. In the Bosnian version it is very difficult to read. Therefore, I would kindly ask the usher to hand a hard copy to the witness. For the record, D 936 is a document of the 1st corps command dated the 3rd of July, 1993. The title is daily combat report. Witness, have a look at the document, its first page, you told us that you were a member of the 3rd corps command. Please look at the right-hand side where the distribution list is. It says the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina armed force Supreme Command staff and underneath we have the IKM of the RBiH armed force Supreme Command Staff at Zenica. Can you tell us why you sent this document to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Because at that time the Supreme Command staff headed by Commander Delic had established its forward command post in Zenica. In order to keep our superior command informed about all of the event, which sent this document to the IKM as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We were referring to the 1st corps. This is a document of the 1st corps. It seems that you have said the 3rd corps. I was referring to this document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, who headed the Main Staff of the armed forces at Zenica at the time?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: The IKM at Zenica was headed by General Stjepan Siber.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Read out the text for yourself under (A), situation is described therein. General, under (A), I wanted to ask you this. What does this paragraph refer to?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This part of the document talks about the degree or intensity of non-stop shelling on the part of the aggressor aimed at the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is stated that the Chetniks broke through our first defence lines in the wider area of Mujkica Brdo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us where Mujkica Brdo is and can you indicate it on the map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Mujkica Brdo is here approximately, just below the letter S in Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't see where you indicated that. Could you please place an X there and write Mujkica Brdo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 3rd of July, 1993, we here see that the Serb forces broke through into a part of Sarajevo that had been controlled by the units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 3rd of July, 1993, what did that mean for the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: It meant that the city would fall. It meant that the aggressor would manage to cut the city in half and to destroy the Istok facility. Since it was a crucial location the whole outcome of the war would be put into question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: As the corps command, did you study that situation with the Main Staff? Did it deal with the situation?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes. It studied it, because, at that time, it was also a strategic task for the staff of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say a strategic task, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I mean that they had to deal with it and to leave everything else aside, as unimportant at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they had to deal with that, what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: They had to deal with the defence of Sarajevo so as to defend the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please assign an Exhibit number to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: D936 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit number 1325.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please be shown Exhibit 229 at this moment. For the record, it is a Supreme Command staff document from its intelligence administration dated the 17th of July, 1993. The title is: Weekly report, military operational situation at the front lines in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the first part of the document. I'm talking about the military operational situation and specific events in the theatre in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the past week. Please tell us which of those listed took place within your corps area of responsibility, that is in Sarajevo and its immediate surroundings?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: In my AOR, that is the AOR of the 1st Corps, we have the first item, that is, the offensive against Rogoj and Trnovo; and then item 2, offensive at Mount Igman; item 3, concentration of aggressor forces in the Sarajevo sector; item 6, continuation of combat activities in the Gorazde sector; and item 8, additional mobilisation of the Croatian Defence council.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Does the document reflect ... the items you've just read out, do they reflect the situation in the field. Is that correct, as you know it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to mark Mount Igman on the map.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: This is Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to pause or deal with this document a bit longer. I would like to ask you this. Mention is made here of additional mobilisation of the HVO. Can you tell us, please, this was on the 17th of July, 1993. What were the relations between HVO forces and the BH army at this time; in other words in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: We can answer in one word, the relations were wartime, because the Croatian Defence Council, at the beginning of 1993, launched together with the Croatian army an aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina the same way that the Serb forces did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please remove this document, and I would like the witness to be shown document D935. For the record, this is a document from the 1st Corps command of 1st July, 1993, entitled, "Information on HVO fighter concentration hereby submitted to OG Igman." Would you please take a look at this document. Please, Witness, take a look at the document. It's legible and short. In the first section it deals with the concentration of HVO fighters in Kiseljak, and it then deals with their participation in the fighting around Kiseljak. Would you please just briefly comment on this. Do you remember these events.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this in your area of responsibility or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this actually happening then? Was there a concentration of HVO fighters at that time or not?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please point to Kiseljak on the map and put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Kiseljak is here, the place where I put the circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to show you another document. Let's keep the map where it is for a while longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, I would like to tender document D935 as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: D935 the document is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will be become exhibit number 1326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think at this point I would like to also tender this map with the markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map with the markings on it is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map will become exhibit number 1327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 1247. Could we just scroll down the document to see the author of the document. And could we do the same with the English version. Please display the next page on the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the English page to come up, for the record let me say that this is a document from the command of the Igman defence of 30 July 1993, and I would like to ask you this. Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who authored it?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to talk with you about this date, the 30th of July, 1993, and I will quote the problems that are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see again the previous page of the English version. Please scroll down in the document so that we see the part saying problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: There it says: "I do not have a single man in reserve or to fight with HD. Mass abandoning of positions especially in Trnovo brigade, where it seems to have been impossible to consolidate positions. Mass population exodus in villages, lack of artillery ammunition. Requests urgently send new forces." Could we now see the next page of the English version, please. "Urgently bring new forces, urgently supply artillery ammunition.
